correctness.rationale: A factor with at least two changes contains a specified complete run and so has only one occurrence, ruling out right-speciality. Both constant factors are right-special; the one-change factors 0^a1^b and 1^a0^b are right-special exactly for a≤b and a<b respectively. This gives p(n+1)−p(n)=n+1 from p(1)=2. A factor with at least three changes cannot have its reversal: the internal run lengths are nondecreasing and the only equal adjacent complete runs occur in the order 0^k1^k. There are n−1 reversal pairs with one change. For two changes the flank bounds for both orientations are a,b≤k around 1^k and a,b≤k−1 around 0^k. Choosing the nonpalindromic representative a<b yields T(n) and T(n−1), where T(m) counts a+2b≤m. The generating function for all nontrivial pairs is z²/((1−z)²(1−z³)); its forward coefficient difference at n is floor((n+2)/3), giving floor(n(n+1)/6) pairs. Subtracting from p(n) proves the stated r(n), hence the 2/3 limit. Unbounded runs of both symbols rule out eventual periodicity. The frozen script was inspected, not run; an independent finite-prefix check at n=10 gave p=56 and r=38. Exact all-length validity rests on the proof.
residual_risks: The independent count is a spot check, not a replay of the full bundled range or a formal certificate.

value.rationale: W is a canonical binary example defined by paired increasing runs. Exact ordinary and reflection complexities quantify how reversals are lost, with contributions isolated by change count. The simultaneous formulas provide a usable test case for the role of reversal closure and recurrence in conjectured limit dichotomies, even though existence of an aperiodic 2/3 example is not new.
residual_risks: This nonrecurrent example does not settle a repair requiring recurrence, uniform recurrence, or reversal closure.
